idiom_name: client-minted operation id (idempotency key) plus a receiver-side key/outcome record, or naturally idempotent operation semantics
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: mint one opaque key per logical operation (a random UUID, a request id or a business idempotency key), attach it to every attempt, and persist it with the pending work so a restart resumes the same operation; on the receiver side, record key -> outcome in the same transaction as the business effect, replay the recorded outcome for a duplicate, and reject a replayed key whose parameters differ. Where a key is awkward, change the operation instead: absolute writes (upsert by business identifier, PUT of a full representation), conditional writes guarded by a version or ETag, or set-style updates instead of increments and appends. The retry policy is part of the contract - automatic replay is allowed only for operations declared idempotent (safe methods, PUT/DELETE or keyed commands) - and the key must be passed on to downstream calls, because a guarantee that stops at the first hop is not a guarantee.
code_sketch:
key = uuid4()                        # once per logical operation
loop:
    resp = POST /charges  Idempotency-Key: key    # same key every attempt
    if resp is definitive: break                  # else back off and replay
# receiver, one transaction:
BEGIN
  INSERT INTO keys(key, request_hash, state) VALUES (...) ON CONFLICT(key) DO NOTHING
  if inserted:  apply_effect(); UPDATE keys SET state='done', outcome=...
  else:         return recorded_outcome          # 409 if request_hash differs
COMMIT
pitfalls: A key that is minted inside the retry loop, derived from the payload, or kept only in volatile memory changes what 'the same operation' means and silently disables the guarantee.
The deduplication marker and the business effect must commit atomically; otherwise a crash replays a partially applied operation.
Deduplication expires: retention must exceed the longest redelivery or resubmission window, including manual replays from a dead-letter queue.

Mint the key inside the retry loop: a timeout that fires between the retry call and the HTTP write means the key is generated fresh each time, silently disabling deduplication while the code still looks protected.

Parameter drift on replay: the same idempotency key reused with a different request body – the server must detect this and return 409 Conflict, otherwise a stale outcome is returned for semantically different work.

Low-entropy key collision: keys derived from counters, timestamps, or user-provided strings can collide across distinct operations, causing one logical operation to be silently collapsed into another.

Concurrent duplicate race: two simultaneous retries of the same key both pass the uniqueness check before either commits – requires an atomic conditional upsert with a unique constraint, not a check-then-insert in application code.
In-progress leak: recording a 'processing' state for a key and crashing before either completing or rolling back leaves the operation stuck permanently; requires a timeout-based reconciliation step.
Premature key expiration: keys that expire before a retry can arrive reopen the duplicate window and cannot protect that replay.

Using sensitive or personal data as idempotency keys: email addresses, user IDs, or personal identifiers in keys leak into logs, network traces, and deduplication stores, creating privacy and compliance exposure – use cryptographically random tokens instead.

Non-atomic marker and effect commit: if the deduplication marker and the business effect are written in separate transactions, a crash after the business effect commits but before the marker is recorded means a retry will re-execute the already-committed effect.

Eventual consistency in the deduplication store: a stale read of the key set can allow a duplicate request to pass the uniqueness check before the original write is visible – use strong consistency for high-stakes operations.
Unbounded auto-retry of non-idempotent methods without a key: SDKs or middleware that blindly retry POST requests on timeout without an idempotency key break the guarantee.
Single key for a batch of N items: if one item fails and the retry replays the entire batch with one shared key, all N items are re-executed – each logical item needs its own key.

Assuming the key's deduplication scope matches the retry's scope: a token scoped per availability zone, shard, tenant or table partition does not deduplicate a retry that lands in a different slice of that scope - AWS EC2 surfaces this as IdempotentParameterMismatch, while a per-shard key in an application store fails the same way invisibly.

Testing idempotency with sequential requests only: a check-then-write implementation passes every sequential test and still double-applies when two attempts overlap, because the duplicate window is a race rather than a sequence - replays must be exercised over concurrent connections.

Trusting infrastructure deduplication for effects outside its boundary: broker-level or gateway-level duplicate detection covers only writes inside that system's transaction, so a call to a third-party provider (payment, e-mail, carrier) still needs its own deterministic key and a reconciliation query - a key is a promise about one store, not about the world.
